books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: J. F. Jarvis, 'Coxey's Army approaching Washington,' stereograph, 1894

stimulus.text: Stereograph photograph, “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!” Coxey’s Army approaching Washington, copyright 1894 by J. F. Jarvis. A column of unemployed men marches along a dirt road toward Washington, led by a man on horseback. Banners in the march read “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!” and “Death to Interest on Bonds.” The marchers set out from Massillon, Ohio, on March 25, 1894, and reached Washington on May 1 with about 500 men.
stimulus.source_note: J. F. Jarvis stereograph, copyright 1894, sold by Underwood & Underwood; Library of Congress, LC-DIG-stereo-1s09209. Public domain: photograph published 1894 (pre-1930). Banner wording checked against the image; march dates and numbers follow the standard account of Coxey's Army.

stem: What did Coxey’s Army ask the federal government to do?

options.text: Pay for public works, such as road building, to employ the jobless
Lower the tariffs on imported goods to cut prices
options.misconception: The banners call for money, roads, and jobs, not for lower tariffs.

options.text: Use the Sherman Antitrust Act to break up the trusts
options.misconception: The marchers asked for federal jobs, not for trust-busting.

options.text: Close the gold mines of the West and end gold mining
options.misconception: The marchers wanted more money in circulation, not closed mines.

rationales.A: The banner 'More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!' calls for federal road building and jobs.
rationales.B: The banners call for money, roads, and jobs, not for tariff changes.
rationales.C: The marchers asked for federal jobs, not for action against the trusts.
rationales.D: The marchers wanted more money in circulation, not closed mines.
rationales.general:
Read the banners as the demand.
1. The marchers carry banners reading 'More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!'
2. Good roads meant a federal road-building program to employ the jobless.
3. The marchers were unemployed men walking to Washington to ask Congress for work.
4. Their demand was federal spending on public works, not tariffs, trusts, or mines.
Remember: a march's banners state its demand, so read the banners.
